The story is remarkably cohesive and economical, with every detail contributing to the underlying narrative and emotional arc. The setting (the aging ferry in the autumn fog), the sparse dialogue, and the small character details (Jonas's city shoes and spreadsheets contrasted with Ilse's practical, weathered routine) all work together to paint a clear picture of a mother trying to keep a struggling family ferry business afloat—likely after the death or departure of "Henning"—and her estranged, urbanized son coming home to check on her. 

The beginning establishes the tension (Jonas's unannounced arrival and criticism of the ferry's engine), the middle explores their history and the declining state of the business (counting the meager daily passengers), and the ending provides a quiet, satisfying resolution. Instead of arguing about the ferry's viability or Jonas's intrusion, Ilse wordlessly accepts his presence and invites him back into her world by handing him the mooring line for one last crossing. Every element serves this central, understated reunion.
